content: Lie bumps, also known as transient lingual papillitis or fungiform papillary glossitis, are painful, hypertrophic (enlarged), red and white papillae that appear on the tongue. These lesions are relatively common. A study conducted in 1996 reported that 56% of survey respondents had experienced these lesions. The condition is most frequently observed in young women and typically involves one or several fungiform papillae. The symptoms generally persist for several days and resolve spontaneously without requiring any specific treatment. The term lie bumps originates from a myth suggesting that telling a lie would cause these bumps to appear. However, the actual cause is often attributed to irritation of the tongue's papillae (taste buds) by sharp foods or teeth. Despite this, there is limited scientific literature on the condition, and no definitive cause has been established through research. Potential contributing factors include stress, gastrointestinal upset, menstruation, consumption of acidic or sour foods, and local trauma (direct physical irritation) to the tongue. There is no specific treatment for lie bumps. Pain relief can be achieved by applying ice or using numbing medications. Anecdotal remedies include gargling with salt water and directly applying hydrogen peroxide to the affected area.
